supply_chain_design.label: Practice 2
supply_chain_design.text: One student initiated contact but did not engage substantively with the tutor, making it impossible to assess their understanding of supply chain differentiation strategy, the RCH Industries case, or the spreadsheet modeling components of the work.

supply_chain_design.label: Practice 7
supply_chain_design.text: Students engaged deeply with constraint formulation across combinatorial auction design and supplier allocation problems, with particular focus on demand constraints and supplier diversification requirements. The main area of confusion centered on the distinction between equality and inequality constraints in demand formulation—several students initially defaulted to equality (=) when inequality (≤) was the correct formulation—though tutoring conversations successfully resolved this through targeted questioning. Students also worked through the conceptual differences between forward contracts and options as risk management tools in supply chain contexts, exploring how each addresses price volatility differently. Across all conversations, the tutor effectively used Socratic scaffolding to help students derive constraint logic themselves rather than receiving direct answers, which appeared to deepen their understanding of the underlying optimization principles.

supply_chain_design.label: Practice 8
supply_chain_design.text: Students engaged with working capital metrics and cost accounting methods across several brief conversations. Most interactions centered on cost-to-serve analysis and the cash conversion cycle components (DIO, DSO, DPO), with students working through calculations and conceptual understanding of how these metrics connect. The tutor consistently used Socratic questioning to guide students toward retrieving their own prior work and verifying results rather than providing direct answers, which kept students responsible for their reasoning. Overall, students showed engagement with the material, and the tutor maintained supportive, focused dialogue without introducing confusion or off-topic drift.

supply_chain_design.label: Practice 9
supply_chain_design.text: Students engaged deeply with the core mechanics of capital budgeting and discounted cash flow analysis, with most conversations centering on free cash flow calculation, NPV analysis, and terminal value estimation. The most consistent challenge was distinguishing relevant from sunk costs and correctly identifying which cash flows belong in incremental analysis—students frequently struggled with the "with/without" test when applied to operating expenses, working capital changes, and depreciation effects. A secondary area of difficulty involved perpetuity valuation and the proper treatment of terminal cash flows in discounting, where students sometimes confused which cash flow component to use in the numerator. Most tutoring interactions were effective in using Socratic questioning to guide students through these distinctions, though a few conversations showed the tutor either over-explaining procedural steps or confirming answers without requiring students to show their reasoning first.

supply_chain_design.label: Practice 10
supply_chain_design.text: Students engaged with a broad range of financial analysis topics across the practice set, with most conversations focusing on ratio calculations, working capital metrics, and the Bosna Brothers and Mulcreavy Artisans case studies. The most common areas of difficulty centered on understanding the components and application of profitability ratios (ROA, ROE, margins), correctly identifying balance sheet line items for working capital calculations (particularly Accounts Receivable and Accounts Payable Turnover), and interpreting trade credit terms and discount notation. Several students struggled with the mechanics of average inventory calculation and the relationship between different financial metrics in the DuPont framework. Most tutoring interactions were brief, and the tutor generally employed Socratic questioning effectively to guide students toward self-discovery; however, a few conversations showed instances where the tutor provided formulas or reasoning steps directly rather than prompting students to derive them, and in a small number of cases, near-submission-ready output was generated before students had reasoned through the problem themselves.

ai_edge.label: Exercise 1
ai_edge.text: Students engaged with a wide range of topics across agent design, campaign strategy, and technical setup, with most conversations centering on how to specify and design a Campaign Strategist agent and select appropriate marketing artifacts. Many students struggled with the initial orientation to the assignment—several had minimal or no substantive interaction with the tutor, while others asked off-topic logistics or setup questions that required redirection. Among students who engaged substantively, common areas of confusion included distinguishing between prompt engineering and code implementation in agent design, understanding what constitutes a complete artifact specification, and clarifying the relationship between customer archetypes and campaign deliverables. A few conversations showed strong Socratic scaffolding and diagnostic questioning, though some tutors fell into patterns of re-explaining full assignment context or providing method dumps without first diagnosing what students already understood, and several responses were longer than necessary given the specificity of the student's question.

supply_chain_fundamentals.label: Practice 1
supply_chain_fundamentals.text: Students engaged with a broad range of interconnected topics across ABC segmentation, demand forecasting, inventory classification, and probability-based safety stock calculations. Most conversations were brief, with many consisting of single exchanges where tutors appropriately redirected students to course materials or guided them toward independent verification rather than providing direct answers. The most substantive multi-turn conversations revealed a consistent pedagogical tension: while tutors generally demonstrated strong scaffolding, diagnostic questioning, and supportive tone, several provided near-submission-ready summaries, final numerical answers, or key conceptual insights before students had the opportunity to reason through them independently. The most successful interactions were those where tutors resisted confirming answers upfront and instead asked students to verify their own computations or derive complementary probabilities themselves.
